newsitem.title: USA: U.S. can little afford to expand wheat sales-trade.
newsitem.headline: U.S. can little afford to expand wheat sales-trade.

text.p: The United States can little afford to expand its export wheat sales this year in the face of tight U.S. stocks and big exportable supplies from Europe, Australia and Argentina, U.S. exporters and analysts said.
"We are going to become less and less of an export seller of wheat," a U.S. exporter said.
"We physically do not have as many stocks, we already shipped a majority of our projected wheat exports, and competing origins continue to have big crops and be more aggressive," he added.

The bottom line is that 1996/97 U.S. wheat ending stocks are projected at 435 million bushels, down 35 million bushels from last month because of large exports and domestic use, but up from 376 million bushels for 1995/96.
"This 16 percent increase in ending stocks provides little room for the U.S. Department of Agriculture to restart export subsidies," Brock Associates grain analyst Jeff Wilson said.
He argued that even though the pace of U.S. wheat export sales has slowed, the U.S. does not need very many weekly sales of over 10 million bushels to reach its export target for this year.

U.S. wheat exporters, who have been wrestling with slow farmer selling and lower world prices, said Egypt bought the wheat below U.S. prices. "We knew that would be the case," a second U.S. exporter said.
Soft red winter wheat futures on the Chicago Board of Trade tumbled early Monday with December off 5-1/4 cents at $3.92 a bushel at 1255 CST.
"Things are certainly not rosy for U.S. exports," a third U.S. wheat exporter said. "It is a price issue."
He noted U.S. soft white wheat was around $152.00-$158.00 a tonne FOB, and that U.S. soft red wheat would range from $155-160.00 FOB, all for December shipment.
Egypt bought the French wheat at $149.50-$149.89 a tonne FOB, the Australian wheat at $150.00 a tonne FOB and the Argentinian wheat at $132.50-$134.50 FOB.
The sale would take care of Egypt's needs through January and maybe partway into February, he said.
